title: The Council: where does your stop go?
hook: Where does your stop go? Five legends, two camps.
takeaway: Five legends answer where the stop goes. One camp uses a fixed percent below the buy (O'Neil: 7 to 8%); the other uses the chart (Darvas: just under the range the stock broke out of; Kovner: where the market shouldn't go if you're right, with smaller size). All agree: decide the exit before buying, keep losses small, and go when it hits.
learn: A stop is the price where you sell to take a small loss.
One camp sets it a fixed percent below the buy (O'Neil: 7 to 8%); the other uses the chart (Darvas: just under the range the stock broke out of).
All five agree: decide the exit before you buy, keep each loss small, and go when it hits.
If the right stop is far away, buy fewer shares instead of moving it closer.
question: Where does your stop go?
emotion: the relief of seeing that the greats disagree on the method but agree on the discipline

seats.name: Livermore
seats.answer: If it doesn't rise like it should after you buy, get out.

seats.name: O'Neil
seats.answer: Sell any stock that falls 7 to 8% below what you paid. No exceptions.

seats.name: Darvas
seats.answer: Just under the low of the price range it broke out of.

seats.name: Kovner
seats.answer: Where the market shouldn't go if you're right. Then trade smaller.

seats.name: Seykota
seats.answer: Cut losses. Cut losses. Cut losses.

captions: Livermore watched how a stock acted after he bought.
O'Neil used a fixed line: a small loss, every time.
Darvas set his stop the moment he bought.
Kovner went wider, and bought less to pay for it.
Camp one: a fixed percent below your buy.
Camp two: just under the range it broke out of.

sources.title: Jesse L. Livermore, How to Trade in Stocks (1940), ch. V 'The Pivotal Point' (first-edition record: Bauman Rare Books)

sources.title: Edwin Lefèvre, Reminiscences of a Stock Operator (1923), Project Gutenberg #60979

sources.title: Wikipedia: CAN SLIM (William O'Neil, Investor's Business Daily)
sources.used_for: O'Neil: cut all losses at no more than 7% or 8% below the buy point, with no exceptions

sources.title: Wikipedia: Nicolas Darvas
sources.used_for: Darvas's box method: bought when price broke out of its box and set a stop-loss just under that price at the same time he bought

sources.title: Nasdaq: How Nicolas Darvas used box theory
sources.used_for: cross-check: Darvas placed stop-loss orders just below the lower boundary of the box

sources.title: Jack D. Schwager, Market Wizards (1989), Bruce Kovner interview (reader highlights on Goodreads)
sources.used_for: Kovner, paraphrased: a stop placed where it is hard for the market to reach, with fewer contracts so the dollar risk stays the same

sources.title: Jack D. Schwager, Market Wizards (1989), Ed Seykota interview (as collected by TurtleTrader)
sources.used_for: Seykota, paraphrased: the elements of good trading are cutting losses, cutting losses and cutting losses
